documents.title: Hierarchical Chunking and Vector Search in Production RAG
documents.text: In production Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, chunk size selection presents a fundamental trade-off between retrieval precision and contextual completeness. Standard fixed-size chunking often fragments coherent ideas or introduces irrelevant noise. Hierarchical chunking resolves this dilemma by generating two distinct granularities of text from each ingested document: parent chunks and child chunks. Parent chunks typically span 800 to 1200 words (often set to 1000 words), encapsulating full thematic sections, complete code blocks, or entire conceptual arguments. Child chunks are generated by partitioning each parent chunk into smaller windows of approximately 120 to 180 words (standardized at 150 words) with a small overlap of 20 words to preserve boundary continuity. Dense vector embeddings are computed exclusively for child chunks using sentence transformers like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or text-embedding-ada-002, and indexed into vector databases like Qdrant using cosine distance metrics. When a user submits a query, the dense vector retriever searches over the high-granularity child vectors, achieving high semantic similarity and fine-grained relevance. Once the top child chunks are retrieved, their associated parent_id metadata allows the retrieval engine to fetch the complete parent chunk from relational storage such as PostgreSQL. This ensures that the downstream Large Language Model (LLM) receives sufficient narrative context and surrounding technical details without paying the retrieval dilution penalty of embedding oversized chunks.

documents.title: Hybrid Search: Combining BM25 Keyword Search and Dense Vector Retrieval
documents.text: While dense vector representations excel at semantic matching, paraphrasing, and cross-lingual understanding, they frequently struggle with out-of-vocabulary tokens, exact acronyms, part numbers, function identifiers, and rare technical keywords. Conversely, sparse term-frequency algorithms such as BM25Okapi excel at exact lexical matching, penalizing frequent stop words and rewarding document matches with concentrated rare query terms. Hybrid retrieval unifies dense vector search and sparse lexical search into a single pipeline to achieve state-of-the-art recall across diverse query profiles. In this architecture, an incoming query is concurrently dispatched to a dense vector store (such as Qdrant using HNSW indexing) and a sparse BM25 engine. For sparse search, documents are tokenized by whitespace and lowercase normalization, creating term frequency indices. The two retrieval legs output candidate lists with entirely different score distributions: cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1 (or 0 to 1), whereas BM25 scores are unbounded positive numbers dependent on query length and inverse document frequency. Merging these uncalibrated score distributions directly via arithmetic addition produces severe score distortion. Therefore, modern hybrid search systems employ rank-based fusion mechanisms rather than score-based blending.

documents.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) Mechanics and Parameter Tuning
documents.text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is an unsupervised rank aggregation method designed to combine multiple ranked lists without requiring score normalization or training data. The core principle of RRF is that items appearing consistently near the top of multiple independent search rankings should receive higher combined relevance scores than items ranked highly in only a single list. The mathematical formula for reciprocal rank fusion assigns a score to each item d according to the equation: RRF_Score(d) = sum over lists m of (weight_m / (k + rank_m(d))), where rank_m(d) is the 1-based ordinal position of item d in list m, k is a smoothing constant, and weight_m is a weighting coefficient assigned to retrieval modality m. In standard literature and implementations (such as Cormack et al. and modern RAG pipelines), the constant k is set to 60. The constant k=60 prevents low-ranked outliers in one list from dominating the overall score while ensuring top-ranked matches receive substantial credit. For instance, a first-ranked result receives a reciprocal score of 1/(60+1) = 0.01639, while a tenth-ranked result receives 1/(60+10) = 0.01428. Dynamic weight tuning allows query-adaptive fusion: factual and code queries can assign dense_weight=0.3 and sparse_weight=0.7, whereas conceptual queries allocate dense_weight=0.8 and sparse_weight=0.2. RRF is computationally negligible, executing in sub-millisecond time complexity O(N log N) where N is the total candidate pool.

documents.title: Cross-Encoder Reranking: Precision Optimization over Bi-Encoder Candidates
documents.text: Bi-encoder architectures (standard dense vector retrieval) independently map queries and passages into a shared vector space, allowing millions of documents to be pre-embedded and queried via approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search within milliseconds. However, because bi-encoders compute query and passage embeddings independently, all token-to-token cross-attention between query terms and passage content is lost. Cross-encoder models, such as cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 and BAAI/bge-reranker-large, overcome this limitation by concatenating the query and candidate passage into a single input sequence separated by special separator tokens ([CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP]). Full bidirectional multi-head self-attention is applied across all query and passage tokens simultaneously, capturing nuanced syntactic dependencies, negation, prepositional relationships, and subtle semantic qualifiers. Because cross-encoders cannot precompute embeddings offline, scoring millions of passages is computationally prohibitive. Therefore, high-performance RAG pipelines utilize a two-stage retrieval pattern: a high-recall first stage retrieves the top 20 to 50 candidates using hybrid vector and BM25 search with RRF fusion, and a second-stage cross-encoder re-scores and re-ranks only these top candidates. Output logits are normalized via sigmoid 1 / (1 + exp(-score)), yielding calibrated relevance probabilities, with a threshold filter (typically 0.3) pruning irrelevant results before passing the top-5 chunks to the generator.

documents.title: Agentic LangGraph Workflows, State Management, and Query Rewriting
documents.text: Static single-shot RAG pipelines suffer from failure cascades when the initial user query is ambiguous, poorly formulated, or lacking essential keywords. Agentic RAG addresses this by orchestrating retrieval through state machine graphs using frameworks such as LangGraph. In this architecture, a state graph defines discrete processing nodes and conditional execution edges operating on a shared RagenticState container. The standard flow initiates at a classifier node, which uses an LLM to categorize the incoming prompt into types: factual, conceptual, comparative, procedural, or code, setting adaptive vector and BM25 weighting parameters. Execution then passes to the retriever node, executing hybrid search and cross-encoder reranking. Next, a critic node evaluates the quality and confidence of the retrieved context. If the confidence level is evaluated as LOW and the retry counter has not exceeded the maximum threshold (max_retries = 2), a conditional edge routes execution to a rewriter node. The rewriter node applies Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) to generate an ideal synthetic answer alongside multi-query expansion to produce diverse search perspectives. The synthesized rewritten query loops back into the retriever node for a second retrieval attempt. If confidence is satisfactory or the retry limit is reached, execution proceeds to the responder node to construct the final prompt and stream tokens.

documents.title: Evaluation Methodologies for RAG: Faithfulness, Precision, and Hallucination
documents.text: Systematic evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation requires disentangling the quality of retrieval from the fidelity of response generation. Three core metrics form the foundation of RAG assessment: faithfulness, context precision, and answer relevance. Faithfulness measures whether every claim made in the generated answer can be directly inferred from and grounded in the retrieved context chunks. An answer that introduces external assertions, unsubstantiated statistics, or fabrications receives a low faithfulness score, which directly correlates with the hallucination rate (hallucination_rate = 1.0 - faithfulness). Context precision quantifies whether the retrieved chunks prioritized by the search engine are genuinely relevant to answering the query, punishing irrelevant context that wastes prompt token budget. Answer relevance evaluates whether the response directly addresses the user's inquiry rather than digressing into tangential topics. While automated frameworks like RAGAS rely on multi-stage LLM prompting, custom evaluators can implement structured JSON prompt templates with temperature=0.0 to generate these triad scores per chat turn, enabling continuous tracking of system quality and source degradation over time.

documents.title: PostgreSQL MVCC, Write-Ahead Logging, and Connection Pooling
documents.text: PostgreSQL ensures transactional reliability and high concurrent throughput using Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) and Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). Under MVCC, read operations never lock write operations, and write operations never block reads. When a row is updated or deleted, PostgreSQL does not overwrite the physical data block in-place; instead, it writes a new version (tuple) of the row with updated transaction identifiers (xmin and xmax). Old tuples remain on disk until removed by the VACUUM worker process. To guarantee ACID durability, changes must be written to the WAL before being flushed to shared table buffers. In high-concurrency async Python architectures (such as FastAPI with SQLAlchemy and asyncpg), managing database socket connections requires careful connection pooling. Async engines create a connection pool where worker coroutines borrow connection handles. When asynchronous tasks terminate or encounter event loop shutdowns, unclosed socket handles cause proactor and event loop corruption unless engine.dispose() is explicitly called during task cleanup.

documents.title: Redis Memory Caching, TTL Policies, and Distributed Invalidation
documents.text: Redis provides sub-millisecond in-memory data storage, serving as an intermediate caching layer and message broker in distributed architectures. In hybrid RAG workflows, Redis frequently caches tokenized BM25 search indices and ephemeral session state under partitioned workspace keys (such as bm25:{workspace_id}). Storing serialized chunk lists in Redis avoids expensive database round-trips when generating keyword search indices. To prevent unbounded memory expansion, keys are configured with Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration policies (such as ex=86400 for 24-hour automatic eviction). When workspace documents undergo ingestion or deletion, cache invalidation must be explicitly triggered to purge stale indices. As a broker for Celery task queues, Redis manages distributed background job execution, passing JSON payloads between web worker publishers and asynchronous task consumer daemons.

documents.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE) and Streaming LLM Responses in FastAPI
documents.text: User experience in interactive AI workspaces depends critically on low Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and continuous visual feedback. Standard HTTP request-response cycles require waiting for the entire generation to complete before transmitting the payload, resulting in multi-second perceived latency. Server-Sent Events (SSE) provide a unidirectional, HTTP-compliant streaming protocol where the server pushes text fragments to the client over a persistent connection using the text/event-stream MIME type. In FastAPI, SSE is implemented using StreamingResponse coupled with asynchronous generator functions. Each message is formatted with data: {JSON}\n\n delimiters. In the RAgentic chat pipeline, event generators yield three distinct event types: timeline events (signaling node progress such as classifier completion or retriever status), token events (individual tokens yielded in real-time by LiteLLM streaming), and terminal metadata events (sources used, confidence scores, and calculated evaluation metrics).

documents.title: Celery Asynchronous Task Orchestration and Beat Scheduling
documents.text: Resource-heavy operations such as downloading multi-megabyte PDFs, extracting audio tracks, fetching YouTube transcripts, chunking documents, and calculating cross-encoder embeddings must be offloaded from the synchronous web thread pool to avoid blocking HTTP request handling. Celery provides an enterprise distributed task queue for Python applications. Tasks are decorated with @celery_app.task and dispatched asynchronously via task.delay() or apply_async(). Celery workers consume tasks from Redis brokers, executing long-running pipelines in separate process spaces. Celery Beat provides periodic task scheduling, acting as a distributed cron daemon. In the RAgentic architecture, Celery Beat runs weekly drift detection tasks, inspecting database tables for sources whose rolling average faithfulness score has dropped by more than 10%, automatically flagging degraded sources for re-indexing or administrative review.

documents.title: FastAPI Dependency Injection, Async Handlers, and Pydantic Validation
documents.text: FastAPI leverages Python type hints and Pydantic models to deliver automatic request validation, serialization, and OpenAPI documentation generation. In RAgentic, endpoints in backend/app/api enforce clean separation of concerns through FastAPI's dependency injection system using Depends(). Database sessions are provided via get_db yielding AsyncSession instances, while user authentication is enforced via get_current_user decoding JWT bearer tokens. Incoming chat requests are validated through ChatRequest schemas requiring a query string and optional session_id or source_ids. Asynchronous router handlers (async def) execute non-blocking coroutines, enabling high concurrency by yielding execution during I/O operations such as network calls to vector databases, Redis, or external LLM APIs.

documents.title: LiteLLM Multi-Provider Fallbacks, Circuit Breakers, and Quota Management
documents.text: Production AI applications relying on external LLM APIs face transient rate limits (HTTP 429), per-minute quota exhaustion, and service outages. To ensure high availability, the RAgentic client implements a tiered model ladder and circuit breaker pattern utilizing LiteLLM. The model ladder configures a primary model (such as gemini/gemini-2.5-flash), a lite fallback model with higher free-tier RPM, an OpenRouter proxy gateway, and a high-throughput Groq endpoint. When a provider returns a confirmed daily quota exhaustion error (limit: 0 or GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProject), the circuit breaker opens for that model with a 3600-second (1 hour) cooldown, immediately bypassing the failed provider on subsequent requests without wasting latency. For transient per-minute rate limits, an exponential backoff retry loop attempts calls up to max_retries=2 with a base delay of 10 seconds.

queries.query: What are the exact word counts and overlaps used for parent and child chunks in hierarchical chunking?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Parent chunks typically span 800 to 1200 words (standardized at 1000 words), while child chunks are 120 to 180 words (standardized at 150 words) with an overlap of 20 words.

queries.query: Which chunks are embedded into Qdrant, and where are parent chunks stored for context retrieval?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Dense vector embeddings are computed exclusively for child chunks and indexed into Qdrant. Parent chunks are stored in PostgreSQL and retrieved using parent_id metadata.

queries.query: Why does dense vector search struggle with exact acronyms and part numbers, and how does BM25 solve this?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Dense vectors struggle with out-of-vocabulary tokens, rare acronyms, and exact identifiers because they compress semantics into continuous vector space. BM25Okapi solves this through exact lexical token matching, rewarding concentrated rare terms.

queries.query: What mathematical formula defines Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), and what is the standard smoothing constant k?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The formula is RRF_Score(d) = sum over lists m of (weight_m / (k + rank_m(d))), where k is a smoothing constant set to 60.

queries.query: How do factual vs conceptual query routing configurations differ in vector and BM25 weights?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Factual queries allocate dense_weight=0.3 and sparse_weight=0.7 (favoring BM25 lexical precision), whereas conceptual queries allocate dense_weight=0.8 and sparse_weight=0.2 (favoring dense semantic vector matching).

queries.query: What is the computational complexity of Reciprocal Rank Fusion?
queries.ground_truth_answer: RRF has a computational time complexity of O(N log N), where N is the total candidate pool across all retrieval lists.

queries.query: How does cross-encoder token-to-token attention differ from bi-encoder retrieval?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Bi-encoders encode query and passage independently so cross-attention is lost. Cross-encoders concatenate query and passage into a single sequence, applying full bidirectional multi-head self-attention across all tokens simultaneously.

queries.query: What mathematical function normalizes cross-encoder output logits, and what threshold filters candidates?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Cross-encoder logits are normalized using the sigmoid function 1 / (1 + exp(-score)), with a standard threshold filter of 0.3 pruning low-confidence candidates.

queries.query: What are the 5 nodes in the Ragentic LangGraph agent workflow in execution order?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The five nodes in the graph are classifier, retriever, critic, rewriter, and responder.

queries.query: Under what condition does the LangGraph critic route to the rewriter node instead of responder?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The critic node routes to the rewriter node if the confidence level is LOW and the retry counter is less than max_retries (retry_count < 2).

queries.query: What techniques does the rewriter node use to generate rewritten queries?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The rewriter node uses Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) to generate an ideal synthetic answer combined with multi-query expansion generating 3 alternative query variations.

queries.query: How is the hallucination rate calculated from evaluation metrics in RAgentic?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The hallucination rate is calculated as 1.0 minus faithfulness (or 1.0 - avg_faithfulness in analytics).

queries.query: What are the definitions of the three custom RAG evaluation metrics?
queries.ground_truth_answer: Faithfulness measures if claims in the answer are supported by context; context precision measures if retrieved chunks are relevant to the question; answer relevance measures if the answer addresses the question asked.

queries.query: Why must engine.dispose() be called after asynchronous database tasks using asyncpg?
queries.ground_truth_answer: engine.dispose() must be called to release all socket connections before the event loop closes, preventing open connections from corrupting subsequent tasks' event loops in Windows proactor environments.

queries.query: What Redis key naming pattern and TTL policy are used for BM25 indexes?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The key pattern is bm25:{workspace_id} with an expiration policy of 86400 seconds (24 hours TTL).

queries.query: What three event types are yielded over Server-Sent Events (SSE) in chat streaming?
queries.ground_truth_answer: The stream yields timeline events (node execution progress), token events (real-time generated text tokens), and metadata/completion events (sources, confidence, done).

queries.query: What is the trigger threshold for Celery Beat weekly drift detection to flag degraded sources?
queries.ground_truth_answer: A source is flagged as degraded if its rolling average faithfulness score drops by more than 10% during weekly Celery Beat evaluation.

queries.query: How does the LiteLLM circuit breaker handle confirmed daily quota exhaustion errors?
queries.ground_truth_answer: When daily quota is exhausted (limit: 0), the circuit breaker opens with a 3600-second (1 hour) cooldown, bypassing that provider on subsequent requests without attempting calls.

queries.query: What is the retry strategy for transient per-minute rate limits in the LLM client?
queries.ground_truth_answer: It uses exponential backoff with max_retries = 2 and a base delay of 10 seconds, doubling the delay on subsequent transient rate limit attempts.

queries.query: What MIME media type and response class are used for streaming chat responses in FastAPI?
queries.ground_truth_answer: FastAPI uses StreamingResponse with media_type='text/event-stream' to push real-time Server-Sent Events to the client.
